speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. To begin evaluating your hypertension, how old are you and have you noticed any headaches, vision changes, or swelling in your legs?

speaker: Patient
text: 5-year-old boy. The patient is presented by his mother for a well-child visit. The boy was born at 39 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery, is currently up to date on all vaccines, and is meeting all developmental milestones. His mother reports that he has been generally doing well with no concerns. No family history of cardiovascular disease. The boy does not take any medications.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for the information. Since you are a 5-year-old with new-onset hypertension and no family history, we need to investigate potential secondary causes. Have you noticed any unusual growth patterns, such as being shorter than expected for your age, or any abdominal pain?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is High blood pressure on the right upper extremity.

speaker: Doctor
text: That is a critical finding; unilateral high blood pressure in a child often suggests a structural vascular issue. Can you tell me if your child has any dimpling or bluish discoloration in the skin between the neck and the abdomen? REQUEST IMAGIS

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: No significant past medical history. Born full term with an uneventful neonatal period. Social history: Patient attends kindergarten. Lives with parents and one younger sibling. No exposure to tobacco smoke.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Coarctation of the Aorta. The finding of significantly higher blood pressure in the right upper extremity compared to the lower extremities, in a young child with no family history of primary hypertension, is pathognomonic for this condition. I request a lower extremity blood pressure measurement and an echocardiogram to confirm the diagnosis.
